```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(mirt)
set.seed(123)
```

## 1. Overview

This report fits graded response models (GRMs) to the 15-item Generic
Conspiracist Beliefs Scale (GCBS; Brotherton, French & Pickering, 2013).
The scale was built around five related facets of three items each:
Government Malfeasance (GM: Q1, Q6, Q11), Malevolent Global Conspiracies
(MG: Q2, Q7, Q12), Extraterrestrial Cover-up (ET: Q3, Q8, Q13), Personal
Wellbeing (PW: Q4, Q9, Q14) and Control of Information (CI: Q5, Q10,
Q15), but it is usually scored as a single total.

This analysis asks the following questions:

1.  Can the items be treated as one latent trait, and is there evidence
    of more than one dimension? (1-, 2- and 3-factor models were
    compared.)
2.  Do items function differently for men and women (DIF)?
3.  Which respondents do not fit the model?

## 2. Data

The data come from the Open Source Psychometrics Project
([openpsychometrics.org/\_rawdata](https://openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata/),
file GCBS.zip). They were collected online in 2016, mostly for personal
interest, so this is a convenience sample (n = 2,495 before exclusions).

Each item is scored from 1 (definitely not true) to 5 (definitely true).
A score of 0 indicates a missing response.

```{r data-prep}
gcbs <- read.csv("data.csv", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Keep gender codes 1 (male) and 2 (female) and the 15 items
gcbs <- subset(gcbs, gender == 1 | gender == 2, select = c(Q1:Q15, gender))

# 0 = missing; listwise deletion
gcbs[gcbs == 0] <- NA
gcbs <- na.omit(gcbs)

gcbs$gender2 <- ifelse(gcbs$gender == 2, "F", "M")
nrow(gcbs)
table(gcbs$gender2)
```

After excluding respondents with missing item responses or a gender code
other than 1 or 2, N = 2,269 (1,086 women and 1,183 men).

## 3. Unidimensional graded response model

```{r mod1}
mod1 <- mirt(gcbs[, 1:15], 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
```

### Item parameters

`a` is discrimination (how sharply an item separates people at different
trait levels). `b1`-`b4` are the trait levels at which a respondent has
a 50% chance of answering at or above each successive category.

```{r mod1-coef}
coef(mod1, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
```

### Loadings

```{r mod1-summary}
summary(mod1)
```

### Global fit

```{r mod1-m2}
M2(mod1)
```

**Interpretation:** The one-factor model showed good global fit: RMSEA =
.043 (90% CI .038–.049), CFI = .97 and TLI = .96. SRMSR = .077 is just
under the .08 guideline. The M2 test was significant, M2(45) = 237.4, p
\< .001, indicating the model does not fit perfectly. With a sample this
large the test is very sensitive to small misfit, so the approximate fit
indices are the better guide.

### Item fit

```{r mod1-itemfit}
itf <- itemfit(mod1)
itf$p.adj <- round(p.adjust(itf$p.S_X2, method = "BH"), 3)
itf

```

**Interpretation:** S-X² values are interpreted alongside the item
RMSEA, because with a sample of this size even trivial misfit is
statistically significant.

Four items (Q7, Q9, Q10 and Q11) had unadjusted p-values below .05, but
the item-level RMSEA values were all ≤ .012, indicating negligible
misfit, and none remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg
correction for 15 comparisons (all adjusted p ≥ .084). No items showed
meaningful misfit.

### Category response curves

```{r mod1-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
plot(mod1, type = "trace", as.table = TRUE,
     auto.key = list(text = c("Definitely not true", "Probably not true",
                              "Not sure", "Probably true", "Definitely true"),
                     space = "right", points = FALSE, lines = TRUE))
```

**Interpretation:** The category response curves show that the response
options are ordered as intended for all 15 items: as belief increases,
the most likely answer moves from “definitely not true” to “definitely
true” with no reversals, consistent with the increasing thresholds
(b1–b4). “Probably true” is the most distinct middle category, whereas
“Not sure” has the lowest peak and is rarely the single most likely
response, so it contributes less information than the other options. The
curves also reflect the item parameters: Q12 has the steepest curves
(highest discrimination) and Q10 the flattest (lowest). The ET items
(Q3, Q8, Q13) are harder to endorse, with curves located at higher
belief levels and overlapping middle categories, whereas Q15 is easy to
endorse, with curves located at lower belief levels.

### Item endorsement for an average respondent

The probability of answering 4 or 5 at the sample mean (theta = 0).

```{r endorse}
endorse <- sapply(1:15, function(i)
  sum(probtrace(extract.item(mod1, i), matrix(0))[4:5]))

endorse_tab <- data.frame(item = paste0("Q", 1:15),
                          p_endorse = round(endorse, 3))
endorse_tab[order(-endorse_tab$p_endorse), ]
```

## 4. Is the scale unidimensional? Exploratory models

Two- and three-factor exploratory models are compared with the
one-factor model.

```{r exploratory}
mod2 <- mirt(gcbs[, 1:15], 2, verbose = FALSE)
mod3 <- mirt(gcbs[, 1:15], 3, verbose = FALSE)

anova(mod1, mod2)
anova(mod2, mod3)
```

```{r oblimin}
summary(mod3, rotate = "oblimin")
```

An oblique (oblimin) rotation is used because the facets are expected to
correlate. A four-factor model was also attempted. It did not converge
reliably (a negative likelihood-ratio statistic against the three-factor
model), so it is not reported; with 15 items and three items per facet,
the data probably cannot support that much structure.

```{r mod4, eval=FALSE}
mod4 <- mirt(gcbs[, 1:15], 4)   # attempted; did not converge reliably, so not run here
```

**Interpretation.** Fit improved significantly from one to two factors
(p \< .001) and from two to three factors (p \< .001). A four-factor
model did not converge, so three factors is the upper limit this item
set supports. In the three-factor oblimin solution, two factors
correspond to complete published facets: ET (Q3, Q8, Q13) and MG (Q2,
Q7, Q12). The remaining items (GM, CI, and PW items Q4 and Q14) load
mainly on a single broad factor. Q9 (PW) loads weakly and about equally
on all three factors, so it doesn’t clearly belong to any of them. The
factors were strongly correlated (r = .61 to .80). Although the scale
was developed with five facets, each has only three items, which may
make them hard to separate in an exploratory analysis. A confirmatory
comparison would be needed to test the published structure directly.

## 5. Differential item functioning (gender)

DIF tests whether men and women with the same level of the trait answer
an item differently. A one-factor graded model is fitted to both groups
with all item parameters constrained equal across groups, and group
means and variances free. Each item is then released in turn (its slope
and four intercepts are allowed to differ) and compared with the
constrained model using a likelihood-ratio test. p-values are adjusted
with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

```{r dif-setup}
items <- gcbs[, 1:15]

mg <- multipleGroup(items, 1, itemtype = "graded",
                    group = gcbs$gender2,
                    invariance = c(colnames(items), "free_means", "free_var"),
                    SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

dif_results <- DIF(mg,
                   which.par = c("a1", "d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"),
                   scheme = "drop",
                   p.adjust = "BH")
dif_results
```

**Interpretation:** In this first pass, 13 of 15 items were flagged,
which can occur when a few items differ and the rest are held equal. A
sequential purification step (using BIC) therefore freed the clearest
items one at a time and retested the rest.

```{r dif-purify}
dif_purified <- DIF(mg,
                    which.par = c("a1", "d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"),
                    scheme = "drop_sequential",
                    seq_stat = "BIC",
                    max_run = 10)
dif_purified
```

**Interpretation:** Only Q3 and Q8 (both ET items) showed DIF (Q3: X²(5)
= 67.7; Q8: X²(5) = 47.1; both adjusted p \< .001). Q13, the third ET
item, was not flagged. To see the direction and size of the difference,
a final model freed only these two items and the group-specific
thresholds were compared (below), followed by expected-score plots.

```{r dif-final}
anchors <- colnames(items)[-c(3, 8)]

mg_final <- multipleGroup(items, 1, itemtype = "graded",
                          group = gcbs$gender2,
                          invariance = c(anchors, "free_means", "free_var"),
                          SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

coef(mg_final, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)




```

**Interpretation:** Men's thresholds were about 0.3–0.4 SD higher than
women's for both items, with similar discrimination, so women were more
likely to endorse them at the same level of overall belief. Separately
from DIF, the latent trait was scaled with women as the reference group
(mean = 0, variance = 1), and men’s estimated mean was slightly lower
(−0.14) with greater variance (1.25).

Plots are created for Q3 and Q8, the only items flagged after
purification (all others were constrained equal across groups). They
show the response difference on the 1–5 scale at each belief level.

```{r dif-plots, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
itemplot(mg_final, 3, type = "score")
itemplot(mg_final, 8, type = "score")
```

**Interpretation:** Only Q3 and Q8 (both ET items) showed gender DIF
after purification. At the same level of overall belief, women were more
likely to endorse them, by roughly 0.3–0.5 response points in the middle
of the trait range. The DIF is statistically clear but moderate in size,
and it affects two of the 15 items.

## 6. Person fit

Person-fit statistics flag respondents whose answers are unusual given
the one-factor model.

```{r personfit}
pf <- personfit(mod1)
flagged <- pf[abs(pf$Zh) > 3, ]
nrow(flagged)
```

A cut-off of \|Zh\| \> 3 is used because \|Zh\| \> 2 flags about 5% of
any sample by chance. Looking at the raw responses of flagged cases:

```{r flagged-responses}
ids <- as.numeric(rownames(flagged))
fr <- gcbs[ids, 1:15]
fr$avg_other <- rowMeans(fr[, c("Q1","Q2","Q4","Q5","Q6","Q7","Q9","Q10",
                                "Q11","Q12","Q14","Q15")])
fr$avg_ET <- rowMeans(fr[, c("Q3","Q8","Q13")])
fr[, c("avg_other", "avg_ET")]
```

**Interpretation: S**ome flagged respondents score low on most items but
high on the ET items (for example, respondent 2154 averaged 1.0 on the
other items and 5.0 on the ET items). A few show the reverse pattern,
scoring higher on most items but low on the ET items (for example,
respondent 2068, 3.6 vs 1.0). This is a descriptive observation, not a
tested result. These respondents were selected because they misfit a
one-factor model, so such patterns are partly expected. Counting how
common each pattern is across all respondents, and screening for
careless responding, would be needed before drawing conclusions.

## 7. Conclusions

- A single-factor graded response model fits acceptably (see M2 above),
  which supports scoring the GCBS as one total.
- More than one dimension is also supported. ET and MG separate clearly,
  consistent with the published facet structure.
- No items showed meaningful misfit: four had unadjusted p \< .05 but
  with negligible effect sizes, and none survived correction for
  multiple comparisons.
- Only two of 15 items (Q3 and Q8, both ET) showed gender DIF after
  purification, with women more likely to endorse them at the same level
  of belief.

## 8. Limitations

- Convenience sample collected online, with no check for careless
  responding.
- Only male and female respondents are included.
- The four-factor model did not converge, so conclusions about
  dimensionality stop at three factors. The published five-facet
  structure was not tested confirmatorily.
- DIF was tested by constraining all items equal and identifying DIF
  items by sequential purification with BIC. Effect sizes were read from
  expected-score plots and not computed formally.

## References

Brotherton, R., French, C. C., & Pickering, A. D. (2013). Measuring
belief in conspiracy theories: The Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale.
*Frontiers in Psychology, 4*, 279.

Open Source Psychometrics Project. (2016). *Answers to the Generic
Conspiracist Beliefs Scale* [Data
set]. <https://openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata/>
